Ecuador is a small country in north-western South America named for the equator, which runs through it. Its capital is Quito, high in the Andes, and its population is about 18 million. Spanish is the official language, and the currency is the US dollar.

It has four regions: the Pacific coast, the Andean highlands with volcanoes such as Cotopaxi, the Amazon rainforest, and the Galápagos Islands, about 1,000 kilometres offshore. There, Charles Darwin studied giant tortoises and finches in 1835, which helped him to develop his theory of evolution.

Quito's historic centre was among the first places to be named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, in 1978. Ecuador is one of the world's largest exporters of bananas and also grows cacao and flowers, especially roses.

articles.title: Bolivia
articles.description: The high Andean country of salt flats and two capitals.
articles.content:
Bolivia is a landlocked country in central South America. It has two capitals: Sucre, the constitutional capital, and La Paz, the seat of government, which at about 3,650 metres is the highest administrative capital in the world. The population is about 12 million. Spanish and 36 indigenous languages, such as Quechua and Aymara, are official, and the currency is the boliviano.

The Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat, covers about 10,000 square kilometres and turns into a giant mirror after rain. It also holds huge deposits of lithium, used in batteries. Lake Titicaca, shared with Peru, lies on the border.

Bolivia lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific in 1879–1884. The ruins of Tiwanaku are a pre-Inca site, and the silver mines of Potosí were once among the richest in the world.

articles.title: Uruguay
articles.description: A small South American country with a big football history.
articles.content:
Uruguay is a small country in South America, between Argentina and Brazil, with its capital in Montevideo and a population of about 3.4 million. Spanish is the official language, and the currency is the peso. It has gently rolling grasslands and Atlantic beaches, including the resort of Punta del Este.

The country gained independence in 1828. It hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930 and won again in 1950. Uruguay is known for its gaucho cowboy tradition, beef and the drink mate, a herbal tea that people carry in a gourd.

Uruguay is regarded as one of the most stable democracies in Latin America. In 2013 it became the first country to legalise the regulated sale of cannabis nationwide. Its Carnival, which lasts over 40 days, is said to be the longest in the world.

articles.title: Costa Rica
articles.description: A green Central American country of rainforests and pura vida.
articles.content:
Costa Rica is a small country in Central America with coasts on the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea, with its capital in San José and a population of about 5.2 million. Spanish is the official language, and the currency is the colón.

The country abolished its army in 1948 and put the money into education and health. Costa Rica has only 0.03% of the Earth's land area but is home to roughly 5% of the world's species. About a quarter of its land is protected in national parks and reserves, and ecotourism is a leading industry.

Almost all of its electricity comes from renewable sources such as hydropower, geothermal and wind. Coffee and bananas are major exports, and the national motto, pura vida, means pure life. Its volcanoes include Arenal, and sea turtles nest on its beaches.

articles.title: Jamaica
articles.description: The Caribbean island of reggae, Blue Mountain coffee and sprinters.
articles.content:
Jamaica is an island country in the Caribbean Sea with its capital in Kingston and a population of about 2.8 million. English is the official language, but most people also speak Jamaican Patois. The currency is the Jamaican dollar. It gained independence from Britain in 1962.

The island is famous for reggae, which came from Kingston in the late 1960s, and its best-known star, Bob Marley. The Rastafari movement also began in Jamaica. Blue Mountain coffee is among the most prized in the world, and the spicy jerk seasoning is a national dish.

The Blue Mountains rise to more than 2,200 metres, and the island has waterfalls and beaches. For its size, Jamaica is a sporting giant: Usain Bolt set the 100 metres world record of 9.58 seconds in 2009. The island also entered a bobsled team in the Winter Olympics in 1988.

articles.title: Australia
articles.description: The island continent of unique wildlife and vast outback.
articles.content:
Australia is a country that covers the entire continent of Australia and the island of Tasmania, and it is the sixth-largest country in the world. Its capital is Canberra, and its largest cities are Sydney and Melbourne. The population is about 27 million, and English is the main language. The currency is the Australian dollar.

The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived on the continent for at least 60,000 years, one of the oldest continuous cultures in the world. Modern Australia was formed when British colonies federated in 1901. Most people live along the coast, while the centre is a dry region called the Outback, where Uluru, a sacred sandstone monolith, stands.

The country is home to unique animals such as kangaroos, koalas and platypuses. The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef system in the world, and the Sydney Opera House is one of its best-known buildings.

articles.title: New Zealand
articles.description: An island nation of dramatic landscapes and Māori culture.
articles.content:
New Zealand is an island nation in the south-western Pacific, made up of two main islands and many smaller ones, with its capital in Wellington and a population of about 5.2 million. English, Māori and New Zealand Sign Language are official languages, and the currency is the New Zealand dollar.

The Māori arrived from Polynesia about 700 years ago and call the country Aotearoa, often translated as land of the long white cloud. New Zealand became a British colony in 1840, after the Treaty of Waitangi. In 1893 it became the first country in the world to give women the right to vote in national elections.

The landscapes range from volcanoes and geysers to fjords and glaciers, and were used for The Lord of the Rings films. The kiwi, a flightless bird, is its symbol. Sheep greatly outnumber people, and the All Blacks rugby team performs the haka before matches.

articles.title: Papua New Guinea
articles.description: A land of rainforests and more than 800 languages.
articles.content:
Papua New Guinea occupies the eastern half of the island of New Guinea and many smaller islands in the south-western Pacific. Its capital is Port Moresby, and its population is about 10 million. The official languages are English, Tok Pisin and Hiri Motu, and the currency is the kina.

It is the most linguistically diverse country in the world, with more than 800 languages spoken by different communities, many of them in remote mountain valleys and along rivers. Most people live in villages and rely on farming, and traditional customs remain strong. The country became independent from Australia in 1975.

Its rainforests contain birds-of-paradise, tree kangaroos and huge numbers of insects. The Kokoda Track, a World War II battle trail, is a popular trek. Coffee, palm oil, gold and gas are major exports.

articles.title: Fiji
articles.description: A Pacific archipelago of coral reefs and warm hospitality.
articles.content:
Fiji is an island country in the South Pacific made up of about 330 islands, of which around 110 are inhabited. Its capital is Suva, on the largest island, Viti Levu, and its population is about 930,000. English, Fijian and Fiji Hindi are official languages, and the currency is the Fijian dollar.

The islands gained independence from Britain in 1970. The population includes indigenous Fijians and many people of Indian descent, whose ancestors came to work on sugar plantations in the 19th century. Fijian culture is known for the kava ceremony, in which a mildly sedative drink is shared, and traditional firewalking.

Coral reefs, white beaches and lagoons attract divers and tourists. Rugby is the national passion, and Fiji won the first Olympic gold medal in rugby sevens at the 2016 Rio Games.

articles.title: Paraguay
articles.description: A landlocked heart of South America with two official languages.
articles.content:
Paraguay is a landlocked country in the centre of South America with its capital in Asunción and a population of about 6.9 million. Both Spanish and Guaraní are official languages, and most Paraguayans speak Guaraní, an indigenous language, which is rare in Latin America. The currency is the guaraní.

The Paraguay River divides the country into a fertile eastern region and the dry Chaco plain in the west. The Itaipu Dam, on the border with Brazil, is one of the largest hydroelectric power stations in the world, and Paraguay exports much of the electricity it produces.

In the 17th and 18th centuries, Jesuit missions built settlements in the region, and their ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The traditional drink is tereré, cold yerba mate tea, and the harp is the national instrument.

articles.title: Guatemala
articles.description: The heart of the Maya world in Central America.
articles.content:
Guatemala is a country in Central America with its capital in Guatemala City and a population of about 18 million. Spanish is the official language, and about 20 Maya languages are also spoken. The currency is the quetzal, named for the colourful national bird.

The country was the heart of the ancient Maya civilisation, and Tikal, a great city in the northern rainforest, has pyramids that rise above the jungle canopy. About 40% of Guatemalans belong to Maya groups, and many wear traditional hand-woven clothing with bright patterns.

Guatemala has more than 30 volcanoes, some of them active, and lakes such as Lake Atitlán, surrounded by volcanoes. The colonial city of Antigua Guatemala is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Coffee, bananas and sugar are important exports.

articles.title: Panama
articles.description: The isthmus that connects the Atlantic and the Pacific.
articles.content:
Panama is a country on the narrow isthmus that joins North and South America, with its capital in Panama City and a population of about 4.4 million. Spanish is the official language, and the currency is the balboa, although the US dollar is used in daily life.

The Panama Canal, opened in 1914, cuts across the isthmus for about 80 kilometres, allowing ships to pass between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans without sailing around South America. It was expanded in 2016 with new, larger locks. Around 5% of world maritime trade passes through it.

Panama City has a modern skyline of skyscrapers and the historic district of Casco Viejo, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The country's rainforests, islands and coral reefs are rich in wildlife. The so-called Panama hat actually originated in Ecuador but was shipped through Panama.

articles.title: Cambodia
articles.description: The land of Angkor Wat and the Khmer Empire.
articles.content:
Cambodia is a country in Southeast Asia with its capital in Phnom Penh and a population of about 17 million. Khmer is the official language, and the currency is the riel, although the US dollar is widely used. It is centred on the Mekong River and the great lake Tonlé Sap, which swells and shrinks with the seasons.

The Khmer Empire ruled much of Southeast Asia from the 9th to the 15th century. Its greatest monument is Angkor Wat, built in the 12th century under King Suryavarman II, the largest religious monument in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992. It appears on the national flag.

Cambodia became independent from France in 1953. In 1975–1979 the Khmer Rouge regime caused the deaths of about two million people, and the country has since rebuilt. Today tourism, textiles and rice farming are important.

articles.title: Maldives
articles.description: A chain of coral atolls in the Indian Ocean.
articles.content:
The Maldives is an island nation in the Indian Ocean south-west of India, made up of about 1,190 coral islands grouped into 26 atolls. Its capital is Malé, and its population is about 520,000. Dhivehi is the official language, and the currency is the rufiyaa.

It is the lowest country on Earth, with an average height of about 1.5 metres above sea level, and its highest natural point is only about 2.4 metres, so rising sea levels threaten its future. The islands gained independence from Britain in 1965. Islam is the state religion.

Turquoise lagoons, white beaches and coral reefs make it a major luxury tourism destination, with resorts on private islands. Fishing, especially for tuna, is the traditional industry.

articles.title: Bhutan
articles.description: The Himalayan kingdom that measures Gross National Happiness.
articles.content:
Bhutan is a small kingdom in the eastern Himalayas between India and China, with its capital in Thimphu and a population of about 780,000. Dzongkha is the official language, and the currency is the ngultrum. Most people follow Vajrayana Buddhism, and monasteries and fortresses called dzongs are found across the country.

The country is famous for Gross National Happiness, a philosophy of development that values well-being and culture alongside economic growth. Bhutan protects its environment: more than 70% of its land is forest, and it absorbs more carbon than it emits. Television and the internet were only introduced in 1999.

Its most famous sight is Paro Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest, a monastery clinging to a cliff about 900 metres above the Paro Valley. Archery is the national sport, and people wear traditional clothes, the gho for men and the kira for women.
